entry.title: Brian Evenson Will Mess With Your Head
entry.summary: Brian Evenson’s first book, a story collection titled Altmann’s Tongue, came out in 1994. It was not widely reviewed. The few notices the book did receive in the media ranged from the curious, to the baffled, to the outright disturbed. “In a capsule review, the Los Angeles Times nervously conceded that ‘there is a talent here,’ albeit, ‘an eldritch one,’” noted Ben Ehrenreich in an essay about Evenson’s work that appeared in The Believer. One reviewer, though, an anonymous one, was unequivocal in their dismay over the book’s violent content, which included dismemberment, mutilation, insects placed in the mouths of corpses, and defenestration, among other indignities. “I feel like someone who has eaten something poisonous and is desperate to get rid of it,” wrote the nameless critic. This particular review would prove enormously consequential for Evenson’s career—indeed, for his life. It did not appear in a journal or a newspaper. It was not even published, technically. Rather, it was sent to Evenson’s employer, a university, triggering an inquiry that would lead to his dismissal. The nameless critic was a student at Brigham Young University, the flagship institution of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, located in Provo, Utah, where Evenson taught for the good reason that he was a devout Mormon, raised in the faith his whole life. The student wrote to the university out of concern that a violent, disturbing book like Altmann’s Tongue was not the sort of literary work that good Mormon professors should be pursuing. Over the course of the long and involved inquiry process, Evenson was presented with a choice. If he wished to continue working at BYU, he would have to stop writing books like that. If he didn’t stop, he would have to leave.

entry.title: A Cool Night
entry.summary: Drew Magary’s Thursday Afternoon NFL Dick Joke Jamboroo runs every Thursday at Defector during the NFL season. Got something you wanna contribute? Email the Roo. You can also read Drew over at SFGATE, and buy Drew’s books while you’re at it. I have another soccer game to attend. This has been a parental duty for me and my wife ever since our son got into the sport sometime around the age of zero. You have kids, and you soon realize that the bulk of your time will be spent driving them places. As such, my wife and I have spent the past 17 years driving our son to soccer practice, soccer meetings, soccer games, and soccer team pizza parties. We’ve done this without malice, but the practice can’t help but turn a bit rote when you’ve been doing it for as long as we have. That’s been especially true during the boy’s senior year of high school. This year, he finally made the varsity team. No small accomplishment, but one that requires a great deal of his time and, by association, ours. Practices every day. Two games a week, some of them on the road, all of them extending relatively late into the evening. At one point, his team played a streak of half a dozen games that went to extra time; many of these were played in the rain, which I found extra rude. Some nights, he’s had to do his homework after coming back late from these games. Thus, the schedule is so demanding that the games, for any parent, can begin to feel like a bit of obligation.

entry.title: Basketball Game Interrupts Shit-Talk Session Between Luka Doncic And Yaxel Lendeborg
entry.summary: For months, I've seen Michigan basketball fans chortle ominously about the big personality of Yaxel Lendeborg, the super-senior who led the Wolverines' 2026 national championship run then sidled over to the NBA draft, where he was selected at No. 11 by the Golden State Warriors. They'd murmur something about him being blunt, being goofy, the world isn't ready for him, etc. Sure. I knew the backstory: Born to parents who had both played basketball for the Dominican Republic's national teams, Lendeborg barely participated in organized basketball for most of his schooling because he couldn't keep his grades up, preferring instead to play video games all day, and had no intention to play college ball until pushed by his mom to play in a showcase for Dominican players at the end of high school. His highlights there won him the last scholarship slot at Arizona Western College, and after a cumulative six seasons of college hoops, a first-round NBA draft selection, a Summer League MVP, and a strong preseason, he started at power forward in his NBA debut on Wednesday. A remarkable sequence of events. The Warriors targeted 24-year-old Lendeborg rather than taking a younger prospect, presumably because they wanted a fresh-out-of-the-box starter to retain a competitive team around Steph Curry. It's a noble thought, but at least one game in, with Jimmy Butler still months away from a return after ACL repair, and Kristaps Porzingis reportedly considering retirement due to chronic illness, the Warriors look dismal. While they were getting shredded by the Los Angeles Lakers, 127-105, Lendeborg exchanged lots of animated words and gestures with inveterate shit-talker Luka Doncic. Just before the halftime buzzer, Doncic banked in a half-court shot over Lendeborg, and the two resumed barking at each other.

entry.title: It’s Hard To Be A Rich Radical
entry.summary: Welcome to Listening Habits, a column where I share the music and musical topics I’ve been fixated on recently. What could compel someone to spend four hours on a YouTube essay mostly about the rapper Killer Mike, a B-tier Dungeon Family affiliate who parlayed success as one-half of Run The Jewels to become a B-tier rap A-lister? In truth, it is no worse than sitting through six hours of self-assigned Super Bowl performer Jay-Z and Rick Rubin yap about rap and also therapy. Or watching a three-hour documentary on disgraced Silicon Valley fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in a hilariously, extremely sold out theater. Or watching four hours of Nick Saban coaching propaganda. Or one hour of an ESPN soft focus profile of Ben Simmons that tries to sidestep the question of Simmons’ work ethic. I watch a lot of nonsense I guess it’s safe to say—and people are apparently greatly long-winded. Maybe a better question is who would actually be compelled to make a four-hour YouTube video on Killer Mike? For that answer, we’d have to get into who FD Signifier is and who Jared Ball is, and the importance of the latter’s book The Myth And Propaganda of Black Buying Power. Then we would have to talk about Black leftist politics and anticapitalist critique and how exactly we got to a point where a bunch of people think Killer Mike is at war with black activist streamers and content creators and shooting at them in random freestyles.

entry.title: Dave Pearson: blogmore.el v5.4.0
entry.summary: I've just made a very small update to blogmore.el to fix a small bug, and also to update some deprecated code. The blogmore-new command inserts the result of expanding a template into the buffer when making a new post, and I've not touched that template since I started writing blogmore.el. This includes not updating it when I switched much of the frontmatter-handling code over to proper YAML parsing. The problem here was that the title didn't get quotes around it, which became an issue if there was something like a : in the title; any subsequent attempt to modify frontmatter properties would throw an error. So this release ensures that the title and the date get quoted right away. I guess, at some point, I should rework this code so that it uses the frontmatter-handling code to set up those properties and, instead, just uses the template for the main body. I've also changed all uses of things like when-let and if-let to use when-let* and if-let*. It seems that, as of Emacs 31.1, the former are deprecated.

entry.title: The Dream Are Making Bully Ball Literal
entry.summary: There's a sequence from the first quarter of Game 3 of the WNBA Finals, in which the Atlanta Dream walloped the Golden State Valkyries by a score of 97-71, that would still be grinding my gears if I were a Valks fan. Angel Reese, fresh off her Game 2 masterpiece, started Game 3 aggressively, going right to the rim. She scored the first two points of the game on a nifty duck-in, and then tried to drive on Kiah Stokes on two straight possessions. Stokes blocked her both times, and then blocked a Jordin Canada layup. And then, with just over five minutes left in the quarter, Stokes was subbed out of the game. One of the most noticeable subplots of these Finals is what Reese is able to do when Stokes is and is not matched up with her. When defended by Stokes, she has sometimes struggled to reliably get off clean shots; against every other big on the Valks' roster, she has enjoyed a feast of layups and fouls. Things were no different on Wednesday night: As soon as Aminata Gueye subbed in for Stokes in the first quarter, Reese went straight at her for a bucket and a foul. When Stokes was subbed out again with 7:23 left in the second quarter, Reese got right back to work by hitting a three in Gueye's face and then bumping her out of the way for another layup. The Valkyries and Dream are stylistically similar in a number of meaningful ways, but one area where they diverge is their depth. Golden State has ridden its 10-player rotation to the Finals by believing in every player's ability to contribute, and by prioritizing meaningful amounts of in-game rest for the starters. The Dream, meanwhile, are happy to share minutes among just seven players. A deep roster full of talented players is the kind of thing that can help carry a team through the regular season and a long playoff run, but a dogmatic commitment to using a big rotation can make it harder to navigate that other all-important principle of playoff basketball: matchups.

entry.title: Irreal: A Small Improvement
entry.summary:
really hate being spied on by web sites and other on-line entities. I’m pretty sure this misbehavior won’t be legal much longer but I’m equally sure that the on-line advertising industry won’t go gentle into that good night and will find ways to nibble around the edges of whatever laws get passed.
Happily, there’s Magic Lasso which pretty much solves the problem for Safari users. That would be the end of the story except that I use XWidgets with mu4e to read HTML emails and Elfeed entries through the wonderful elfeed-webkit. They work nicely but now Magic Lasso is no longer filtering their content so cookies and trackers are being accumulated. For the longest time I couldn’t find where they were being stored. I finally stumbled on its location and discovered that it was a simple text file that could simply be deleted.
The problem was that I had to remember to do it and more specifically, where the file was located. I finally stopped being stupid and wrote a simple function to delete the file:
(defun jcs-kill-cookies () "Delete the cookies from Webkit" (interactive) (delete-file ".emacs.d/url/cookies") (message "Cookies deleted."))
jcs-kill-cookies when I quit elfeed so I don’t have to remember to do it manually. All of this is trivial, of course, but it’s another example of sanding down your workflow to make it as simple as possible. Now things pretty much take care of themselves. I suppose I should figure out a way to delete cookies after email too but for now I’m happy that the problem is mostly solved.

entry.title: Irreal: Debugging Init.el Files
entry.summary:
about debugging your init file. The main problem, he says, is that he sometimes makes a change that results in unbalanced parentheses. Often he doesn’t discover this until the next time he reboots Emacs, something he doesn’t do often.
He says that his usual method for finding the problem was to do what amounts to a binary search on his init file: He comments out half the init file. If the problem occurs, he repeats the process with the commented potion; otherwise he continues with the uncommented half. But then he discovered the built-in function check-parens that checks for unbalanced delimiters in the current buffer. That’s a nifty solution to Ridenour’s problem that I didn’t know about. Another tool in the toolbox.
The other thing about his post is that it reminded me of a package I wrote about in 2015 from Artur Malabarba: elisp-bug-hunter. I haven’t used it in a while but every time I do, it works perfectly and invariably finds the error often without any further action. What it does is automate the binary search that Ridenour used to hunt down his unbalanced parentheses but it works for any problem.
If the problem throws an error, elisp-bug-hunter will find it without any user input but for more complicated situations, you can specify a predicate to indicate whether the current run succeeded or not. I load it early in my init so it will be available if there is a problem.
So the take away from this post is two really useful debugging tools: check-parens for finding unbalanced delimiters and elisp-debug-hunter. Everyone should know these tools.

entry.title: Irreal: Updating Clock Tables
entry.summary:
has an interesting problem whose solution is harder than you think it would be. The problem is pretty simple: Every Sunday morning when he writes his weekly review, he needs to update all the clock tables in his journal. That usually takes about a minute and mbork had the idea that he could use an idle timer to run the update. Specifically, he reasoned that if Emacs were idle for a minute it probably meant that he was otherwise engaged and that Emacs would be idle for another minute so why not fire off his update?
Of course, he wanted to do this only once a week on Sundays so it was a bit more complex than just setting the idle timer. He came up with the idea of setting a (normal) timer for 3 AM on Sunday that would set the idle timer. That didn’t quite work because of a technical issue but he got things working with yet another timer.
You should read his post for the details. His solution is interesting and shows that sometimes even simple things can be harder than we imagined.

entry.title: A searchable archive of everything
entry.summary:
I wrote something down recently, and later I couldn't find it. If you know me, you know why; I put my notes into too many different apps. Once in a while I declare loudly that "I'm using only this app, from now on! I mean it!" and then change my mind a month later. It's just the way I am. This most recent failure was the last straw and finally forced me to deal with it properly. Instead of fixing myself, I built a software crutch. I spent today vibe-coding an indexer and search engine for all of my stuff. Here's the initial version of a web UI:
I also hacked together a TUI and an Emacs package. Those access the data via Tailscale SSH so I don't need to worry about installing things on other machines. Just the wrapper script. Here's the list of sources being indexed (so far): ./archive index baty.net: 1272 items (0.9s) archive.baty.net: 2791 items (1.1s) linux.baty.net: 26 items (0.0s) blot.baty.net: 678 items (0.3s) jackbaty.com: 581 items (0.1s) notes: 2287 items (1.0s) dayone: 2507 items (1.4s) thebrain: 1177 items (0.5s) mail: 1 updated, 0 removed (since revision 43773) (1.6s) duplicates: 786 items in 381 groups (10.2s)
One nice thing about this is now I can search all of my Denote notes from my phone. Everything is plain files and it uses boring, durable tools, so the archive should outlive whichever apps made the content that week. Even an AI layer, if I add one, sits on top of the search instead of being built into it. The database is disposable because it only takes 10 seconds to reindex everything. entry.title: Irreal: Saving Window Configurations
entry.summary:
techhub.social, lispwizard has a short post (or whatever techhub.social calls them) on saving window configurations to registers. He notes how easy it is to save multiple configurations and switch between them on the fly.
Saving window configurations and other data in registers is an extraordinarily powerful technique that all Emacs users should learn and master. There’s a problem, though, when you want to do this programmatically: which register should you use? How can you be sure that your choice won’t conflict with a register that the user has chosen manually for some other task? There are several situations in which I want to run an Emacs function in a single window—Elfeed is an example—and I do that by saving the current window configuration, deleting the other windows, running the required function, and then restoring the previous window configuration but how do I choose a “safe” register to save the window configuration in?
The answer is a trick I learned from Magnar Sveen years ago. Instead of using a letter to name the register, you use a symbol like :saved-windows. That works because when you name a register with a letter, Emacs uses a pointer to its symbol as the register name. Using a symbol name like :saved-windows works because the result is also a symbol pointer.
If you have the need to save something in a register programmatically, this is a good way of doing it. You don’t have to worry about conflicts because the user can not use symbol names for registers interactively.

entry.summary: Org Social is so simple it looks like it was born before the internet. A single plain text file, an editor and a host are enough to interact with other people. To "create an account", you just create a plain text file in any editor. Your "database" is your own hierarchy of posts. Your "algorithm" is however you decide to sort other people's posts. There is no "character limit". Your "server" is any hosting or web server. Your "interface" is your favorite editor. And if you want to "delete your account", you just delete the file. And of course, the syntax is richer than Markdown and just as easy to learn: Org Mode. entry.title: Irreal: Org-ibullets
entry.summary:
a simple package that trades Org mode’s heading stars for UTF-8 bullets. If you’re like me, your first thought is, “Doesn’t that already exist?” Sort of. What already exists is the no longer maintained org-bullets. Cherti’s package is called org-ibullets (note the i).
Cherti explains the differences from org-bullets in his announcement. The TL;DR is that he’s optimized org-ibullets by eliminating redundant computations, eliminated spurious syntax warnings that org-bullets could produce, and made some improvements at the source level.
As I said, the package is simple. It can be used right out of the box but you can customize the list of bullets and their face if you desire. This seems like a very nice package if you’d like to make your Org buffers look a little nicer.

I'm not doing that, and I can't find a way to disable the button. On top of that, they're about to charge a $99/year subscription in order to sync my data to Apple Health.
